On the Orders of the Day:

I
beg to call the government's attention to an article which appears in this week's Financial Post and to ask a question with reference
thereto. The article to which I refer appears under the following headlines:
Offer Land on Hudson's Bay at Dollar an Acre to Cleveland Citizens.
Exploration Syndicate "Sponsored by Canadian Government" Seeks Memberships on Promise of Land Grant from Dominion-Radio Base and Aeroplane Station.
Will Raise no U.S. Flag on Discoveries.
I do not intend to inflict the whole article on the House but I should like to read some extracts from it. I quote:
"An organization of red-blooded Americans, cooperating with the Imperial Canadian government to encourage exploratory operations into Hudson's Bay and the Arctic Circle." This is the way "the Hudson's Bay Exploration Syndicate, Limited" of Cleveland, Ohio, describes itself.
The syndicate literature indicates that it is soliciting memberships at $2 apiece, and every member is promised an acre of land in the islands or territories contiguous to Hudson's Bay, "when, as if the intended land grants are made by the Canadian government to the syndicate."
The Hudson's Bay Exploratory Syndicate describes itsedf as an organization sponsored by the Canadian government and further sponsors for its operations, as listed, include organizations of much power and influence. They are:
"The Royal Geographic Society.
"The Ancient and Honourable Hudson's Bay Company.
"The Canadian Campfire Club of Cleveland.
"The Arctic Club of Cleveland.
"The MacMillan Polar Club.
"The National Geographic Society.
"The National Aeronautic Association.
"The Canadian-American Exploration Society, and many others."
Objects of the Syndicate
The objects of the syndicate are, by their literature, stated to be:
"To promote closer relations between two great Anglo-Saxon neighbours;
"To encourage the discovery of new territory in the Arctic Basin;
"To further co-operation between the United States and Canada in opening up to sportsmen the vast unexplored territory contiguous to Hudson's Bay;
"To establish headquarters an the Belcher Islands in Hudson's Bay for aerial operations into the unknown wilderness of the north;
"To secure accurate information relative to the Eskimos and Indian tribes;
"To found a permanent radio base in Hudson's Bay;
"To open a summer seaplane route from Cleveland direct to Hudson's Bay;
"To develop the spirit of exploration among its members and awaken a new interest in the possibilities of discovery and adventure throughout the largest remaining unexplored territory in the world, comprising upward of two million square miles."
"By special arrangement between the Canadian government and the Hudson's Bay Exploration Syndicate, Limited, a completely equipped radio station will be established by the syndicate on one of the Belcher Islands in Hudson's Bay," it is stated.	"Already plans are under way to acquire
title to the largest fresh water lake, christen the same 'Lake Cleveland' and erect a radio station and se#*-
C.N.R.-Coal

plane base thereon. The lake is 64 miles long, from one to five miles in width and shaped like a hairpin. It is known to abound in fresh seaJl, fish, fowl and game of many kinds.
"With permanent radio and sea-plane headquarters in Hudson's Bay, constant communication with civilization is certain. It will be the most popular hot weather station in America.
"Plans are now under way to secure for the syndicate valuable concessions in the Belcher Island group. It is a sportsman's paradise, comprising about five thousand square miles of wilderness almost wholly unexplored.''
Further with regard to the airplane rate, the promise is made that "By the summer of 1927 the new sea-plane route from Cleveland to Hudson's Bay will be open. Any member of the Hudson's Bay Exploration Syndicate, Limited, can hop aboard at the Cleveland station in the morning, fly across Lake Erie, stop at North Bay on Lake Nipissing for luncheon and arrive at the Syndicate Camp on the Belcher Islands in Hudson's Bay in time for supper."
"The flying distance is a trifle over a thousand miles and the average speed should be 120 miles an hour, making it a delightful and fascinating daylight journey.
"From the syndicate sea-plane base on Hudson's Bay numerous air trips can be made into forests, lake and river regions never seen by white man. The possibilities for the adventurer, the explorer and the sportsman ore beyond comprehension."
Will Raise no Flag
It is assured that:
"By arrangement between the syndicate and the Imperial Canadian government no jurisdictional claims will be made to territory discovered through the efforts of the syndicate or its members, and no attempt will be made to raise the American flag and lay claim to the land for the United States. The syndicate realizes that diplomatic relations with the official Canadian government are at all times essential to its success and therefore yields to Canada the right of possession and ownership to all new (territories resulting from its exploratory operations."
Canada is going to make extensive grants to the syndicate, they state, and it is mentioned tliat for the concession of agreeing not to plant any American flags on any territory "discovered" that:
"In return for this concession the Imperial Canadian government will undertake to grant to the syndicate several large tracts of lands, and groups of islands in the Hudson's Bay region with permission to allot portions of the same to the syndicate members, under and by virtue of a special act of parliament."
Are any such negotiations or proposed arrangements as intimated in this article under way? If not, have any steps been taken to restrain the improper use of the Canadian government's name for advertising purposes?

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, yesterday
my hon. friend from Toronto West Centre (Mr. Hocken) asked a question as to whether a rubber stamped paragraph on an envelope which he sent over to me had the approval nr consent of the government. The House resumed from Tuesday, April 13 consideration in committee of Bill No. 17 to amend the Soldier Settlement Act.-Hon. Mr. Stewart-Mr. Duff in the chair.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, while I have not been fortunate enough to reconcile all the suggestions offered in committee, I have done my best to get as near to them as I possibly could. I would much appreciate, Sir, if you would take the bill subclause by subclause. I may say that in clause 1 of section 68 I have made a slight change to make it clear that where the soldier has sold out his interest we are not dealing with that particular land.
How will it read now?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
It is the third reprint we are dealing with to-day. For the information of the committee, I may say that we replaced the word "abandoned" with the words "who has not assigned or transferred." It was said the meaning was obscure, and we have changed the wording to make it absolutely clear.
On Section 1, 68 (1)-Revaluation of land sold to settlers.
What particular settlers will be embraced by this section who were not embraced in the bill as it was formerly constituted??

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: None. Exception was taken to the word " abandoned," and to make it perfectly clear what we were endeavouring to do, we changed the wording. It embraces all those whose contracts are in existence; that is the point.
Then those soldiers who were forced off the land, by reason of the fact that they could not carry the load, have no chance of getting back and having a revaluation of their land made?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes, provided the land has not been allocated. I do not want to lead the discussion away from this particular section, but under -subsection (k), which has been added to the bill, that provision is made. For the information of the committee I might say that we argue that we have that authority under the bill, but there was a good deal of discussion about it and to put it beyond any question of doubt we drafted section (k).

Then if the particular land which the soldier occupied has been disposed

Soldier Settlement Act
of in some way, as has happened in a great many cases, he has no chance of getting either a revaluation or another piece of land?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Practically
no. I have gone into that question rather thoroughly with the board, and there are innumerable difficulties in the way. He could not even come back as a new settler, and you could not transfer his payments. Where the land is still under the control of the board we can re-establish the settler and make an allowance for any payment on principal, or at least put him in the position he occupied before his contract was rescinded. That is the situation.
Ml-. CLARK: A couple of months ago I brought to the attention of the minister a report appearing in the press to the effect
that about fifty empire settlers had been brought into the Fraser valley and settled on soldier lands. Has the minister investigated that report, to ascertain just what degree of truth was in it and how many empire settlers have been placed upon soldier lands in the Fraser valley?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I am informed that approximately fifty are settled in that particular locality, under the scheme of empire settlement.

The minister then proposes to do nothing whatever for the soldiers who were forced to abandon these lands, despite the fact that the empire settlers have been brought in and given the lands at a valuation much lower than that originally given the soldier settlers.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I am very much afraid that that is the situation. I would be very glad to be able to remedy it if I could, but unfortunately I cannot see any way by which that could be done, in view of the difficulties which present themselves. The board, of course, take the ground that they did not in any case force anyone off these lands, and I can only speak from the report which I received in connection with this matter. I will say very frankly to my hon. friend that there is absolutely nothing to be done in a case of that kind, where the land has been allocated to someone else.
Does not the minister think the government is under a moral obligation to return to those people at least the ten per cent which the government took from them and placed in the public treasury?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I would very much prefer to deal with that matter apart from the question of the revaluation of the
lands. We have the problem now of the men who have stuck through thick and th;n and who are still on the land; there is no question in my mind that our first duty is to them. There are innumerable difficulties in connection with this matter, and I stated very frankly in the beginning that I did not see how we were going to meet every individual difficulty that might arise.

I must submit, Mr. Chairman, that I think we should deal with that question now; the government, took the money from those soldiers and put it into the public treasury; non' they have taken their lands away and if the matter is not dealt with now it will never be dealt with.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
May I ask
my hon. friend if he would suggest that the government pay that amount back to the man who dissipated everything, and who got the government property as well? I just mention that to show how difficult it is to deal with this problem. My hon. friend will at once answer no. Then you have to meet the difficulty of the man who, perhaps through no fault of his own, lost all his money, as against the man who will have a thousand and one claims to the effect that it was not his fault that he lost his investment. I merely mention these to show my hon. friend how difficult it is to deal with a complex question of this character. _

I admit that it is difficult, but it is the duty of the government to deal with difficult questions. When the government undertakes to deal with these questions they should deal with the entire question at once. A great injustice has been done to this class of soldier.

We have canvassed
the whole situation; some hon. members have said the whole scope should be widened, others that it should be restricted. This bill apparently goes as far as the government is prepared to go. We want to see relief given to the returned men on the land, so let us report the bill. The government have the responsibility; let us go as far as the government can go, because the soldiers should and must soon receive whatever measure of relief the government is prepared to give them. I am in favour of some extensions; I would like to see some things provided for which are not included at present, but we have covered the whole ground. The minister is not prepared to accept some suggestions; he has accepted some, so let us report the bill.
Soldier Settlement Act

This question has been before parliament for three or four years, and has always been put off. If we accede to the wishes of the hon. member for Muskoka (Mr. McGibbon) I am afraid we will go on with this bill for another two weeks, with the result that, we will not get any revaluation for the soldiers. Let us proceed with this bill, and if these other cases should be taken up, the House can deal with them afterwards in a separate bill.
Mr. McGIBBO'N:	I think the hon. minister is more interested in the political side of the question than in doing justice to the soldiers.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I have not
a word to say in reply to a statement of that character. It is unfair and quite uncalled for.

I was not referring to
the minister, but to the hon. member for Macleod.

Take the case of a soldier who has been put off the land through default in living up to his agreement, and whose land is sold to a new settler, and the purchase money of the new settler plus the money already paid by the soldier who has abandoned his land amounts to more than the original price of the land; does the soldier settler get any benefit from the resale of his land? What I am getting at is this:	Are there any cases
in which by virtue of the double sale of the land the government is getting more for it than it was originally valued at by the government? Let me put a concrete case:	Suppose a soldie;r purchases a farm for $5,000, and pays off $2,000 of that amount, and then makes default; I am talking of the principal. He is put off his land and his farm is put up for sale and sold to a new man who pays, we will say, $4,000. Does the government get the benefit of that extra $1,000? Does the soldier settler get any benefit from the resale of the land?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I am informed that that is done.
I understand that the government has about $600,000 profit from these land sales. If that is so, it is a scandal. They have no right to make money on the soldiers.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: It is a new question to me, but the chairman of the board informs me that in coses such as my hon. friend has mentioned where more is received for the land than the soldier's indebtedness, he receives the difference.

I am not criticizing the minister in the least, because I know there must

be many things done under the machinery of the act that he is not personally familiar with, but what I am getting at is this:	I understand that there is about $660,000 of a profit as a result of these land deals in connection with the soldier settlers, and I would like this House to have the assurance that there is no soldier who is being exploited, either intentionally or unintentionally, by the government of Canada or by the Soldier Settlement Board.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Under the
provisions of subsection 4 of section 22 of the old act the board have 'been repaying the difference that I have just mentioned to the settler when his land is resold.

One more question. I would like to know just what that $600,00 does represent. Where does it come from? It is a profit, and it must be capable of explanation. It must come out of the soldier somewhere.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
While that
statement is made, I am informed by the chairman of the board that that amount is only a book-keeping surplus, because the losses incurred in the salvaging of the implements and stock more than offset that amount.
It is a profit on the land which is set over against the soldier's indebtedness on implements and stock?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes.

Is a profit in the case of any individual soldier set off against the loss in the case of another soldier, or does every soldier get the benefit of the profit that is made on the resale of his land?
Mr. STEW'ART (Edmonton):	Where the
settler is being salvaged and more is received than the amount of his indebtedness, the board do not appropriate that surplus, but pay it back to him, I can see the difficulty my hon friend has, and I frankly confess it is one that I would have had, but the chairman of the board informs me that while the land shows a profit of $600,000, probably owing to the 10 per cent that was contributed by the soldier, nevertheless the losses on salvaging the implements and live stock more than offset that $600,000, but that does not debar the individual soldier from receiving the difference I mentioned and the board have paid to the individual soldier the difference that arises in that respect.

All I want to know is that
each individual soldier is treated on his own merits, as a separate book-keeping entity.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Yes.

Soldier Settlement Act

I would like to support
the stand taken by the hon. member for Selkirk. I have in my constituency about as many soldier settlers I think as there are in any other constituency, and some of them were settled on as poor land probably as there is in the Dominion. I do not want the committee to think that we have a lot of poor land in my constituency, but unfortunately some of these settlers were settled on poor land. The minister in this 'bill is, I think, endeavouring to meet the situation, and to do justice to the soldier settlers in so far as this House can go. There will be, no doubt, cases of injustice due to the individual circumstances in which these men find themselves to-day. But I believe on the whole the minister has tried to make a workable act which will be in the interest of the returned soldiers, and I would support the stand taken by the hon. member for Selkirk that we should report the bill.

The bill provides that all applications for revaluation must be submitted to the board prior to October 1, 1926, and that they must be made by the settlers themselves. Would the minister consider adding a few words to clause (b) so that it will not be necessary for the settler to personally make application, but that application may be made on his behalf by someone else. If the application has to be sent in personally by the settler, there may be cases where owing to incapacity or temporary absence of the settler hardship will result. In my opinion either the date should be extended to the 1st of October. 1927, or such an amendment as I suggest to permit of applications being made on behalf of the settler should be made.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
There are
several objections to that. In the first place, we cannot act without the personal affidavit of the applicant. Forms will be sent to them all. The only reason we make it October 1 is because, as my hon. friend will readily understand, the board will have considerable difficulty in making collections until this revaluation is adjusted, and that is one thing we had in mind. I would have no objection to extending it perhaps one month, but I think October 1 is ample time for everybody to make application, and even if somebody was missed I cannot conceive that because they were a day late in making application that their case would not be considered. But let us get the application in before the board and the adjustments made, so that payments may continue to come in. My hon. friend knows that interest has been suspended for
the past few years. We would like to get the soldiers who are on the land dealt with and their cases settled in a permanent way ir order that they make their payments to the board and carry on. Naturally it will not bt done until this adjustment is made. That is the reason I made it the 1st of October. J would not like my hon. friend to press foi any change in the provision as to the application. We want it to come direct from the soldier and to be supported by his affidavit.

There does not seem
to be any discretionary power vested in the board to accept applications after that date.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Someone
may make an application a day or two late, but it is necessary to get the applications in as rapidly as possible.

How could the board
accept the application if it was a day or two late? If some discretionary power was vested in the board to meet those cases I would be satisfied.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The bill states specifically that the applications must be in by the 1st October, and I would like very much to have that date remain because I want to get the matter settled. The thing will be unending if we do not get these cases dealt with. Therefore there should be a settlement in order to put the soldier settlers out of suspense and let them know exactly where they stand. There are a large number of soldier settlers who are waiting to see what kind of adjustment they are going to get in order to make up their minds wihether they art going to remain on the land or abandon it. Therefore, the quicker a settlement is reached the better it will be for all parties concerned. Consequently, I should not like to change the date fixed.

I only wished to see
that suggestion ,met as to applications being made on behalf of the soldier settler. There could not be any trouble there.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The application and the affidavit must come from the man himself. I have gone into that point pretty thoroughly. A considerable length of time is allowed in which to do it, and naturally there is a great deal of publicity. Every man who is on the land will know the requirements and will govern himself accordingly.

Will the widows and
children of deceased soldier settlers come unaer the scheme?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes.
I think this bill has been before the House long enough.
Hear, hear.

The bill as it has been amended and altered by the minister suits me as the representative of the constituency of Marquette and, I think, will suit the soldier settlers in that constituency also. I believe that I have as many soldier settlers in my riding as any other hon. member here, and I take the responsibility of supporting the bill in its present form. Now, let us report the measure and pass it.

I hope the two hon. members who have just spoken will forgive us for trying to get some further information. I do not think I have asked any questions so far in regard to the bill, and have not said one word about it. Therefore, I do not think it would be fair for these hon. members to prevent me from gratifying my eagerness for information. Did I understand the minister to say that surplus receipts had been paid to soldier settlers?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes.

In what provinces
do the ex-soldiers live who received surplus receipts?

man and will be very glad to do so. My hon friend (Mr. Ross, Kingston) wanted the names of the provinces in which repayments had been made to soldier settlers and also the amount of such payment. We did not come prepared to give that definite information, but I will be very glad to obtain it and furnish it to my hon. friend.

I am not going to discuss the question, I simply wish to get information. It will be understood that many of these ex-service men have suffered. They had to pay 10 per cent of the whole amount that was paid them as a gratuity. A great many of them put up all their savings and then, on account of reasons applicable to themselves or to the department, they absolutely lost every cent they had. speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I pointed
out a few moments ago that that $600,000 really did not exist because the loss on equipment much more than covered the amount paid on the land. What I want to impress upon hon. gentlemen is the fact that where an individual soldier had a balance coming to him he received it.

I want to
press for such a measure of relief for these returned men as the government is willing to give. I think all of us concede the principle that there should be a revaluation. That is acknowledged in the bill itself. Then the question arises: To whom shall the benefit of a revaluation of soldier settler lands accrue? The bill as originally drafted provides that the benefit of revaluation shall extend in the first place to those who are still on the land. That was a very practical measure of relief. As redrafted the bill now extends the privilege of revaluation to those who, having bought lands, left them because of the in-[DOT]flated value and whose farms have not yet been disposed of. The benefit of the bill has been extended in that regard by the insertion of sub-section (k). That is a further measure of relief. I am entirely in accord with that relief so far as it goes. I think that to a great extent it gives relief in a practical way to most of those who are desirous of carrying on on the land immediately.
It does not, however, grant relief in two other classes of cases and to these I wish to refer. First, the case of the soldier settler who has paid up in full. No relief under the revaluation by way of a re-

Soldier Settlement Act
fund is provided for him. I think that is unjust. Let me give two cases by way of illustration: X has a farm on one side of the road which he purchased under the soldier settlement scheme for $7,000. Y, on the opposite side of the road has also purchased a farm for $7,000. We will assume that both farms are of the same value. X has paid up in full. Y still owes $3,000. Both farms were originally bought for settlement. Under this revaluation plan, if Y's farm is revalued at $5,000 he will get a reduction of $2,000. But X, although he paid $7,000 'in full, whether by borrowing or otherwise, will not get any benefit. That is unjust. I urge that men in this class should be given the benefit of revaluation. But the minister has told the House that it is not the intention of the government to go that far. The question has been fully discussed, he says, and they will not go as far as that. Well, I am for accepting from this government what we can get and the responsibility for that injustice must rest upon them.
There is one other class of cases. Take the	men who abandoned	their
farms by reason of the fact that they were carrying too heavy a load. Subsequently their farms, having been salvaged, have been resold to empire settlers, civilians, or somebody else. Such a settler's farm having been sold he cannot come in under this scheme or secure another farm. Personally, I think he should be permitted that privilege. But the bill does not go as far as to take in that class of cases, and the minister has intimated that the government cannot extend that right to them. I take it that the government is prepared to accept that responsibility also. However, I am in accord with the bill in so far as it goes. The matter has been very fully discussed, and if the government, after having these other classes of cases pointed out to them, will go no further than the bill provides for, let us go ahead, make some progress and get such measure of relief as it is possible to obtain at the present time.

I understand we have discussed the' principle of the bill; we are now considering the re-drafted clauses and I must strongly object to the railroading of the bill through while we are considering these clauses.

No, the whole thing will depend on how the form is prepared. It is a matter of detail.

I am not dealing with that
point. I am dealing with the drafting of the bill. The bill provides that the application shall be supported by affidavit supplied by the board, and secondly by a written statement by the .settler, which is not necessarily an affidavit at all. I suggest there should be one affidavit, setting forth the whole of the subject matter that the settler is submitting as the ground for his revaluation.

I endorse what the hon.
member has just stated; and furthermore I point out that the requirement that the affidavit shall be on forms supplied by the board puts the soldier to unnecessary inconvenience. The minister said that the board would send the forms to the soldiers. Many soldiers will not get them and many who get

them will mislay them. Why could the section not read like this:
The application shall be supported by affidavit setting forth the settler's belief as to the present value of the land, his reasons therefor and the names of the persons whom he proposes to call as witnesses.
I presume that is all that is necessary. Why should there be a statutory requirement that the affidavit shall be on a form supplied by the board? It would not be so bad if the settlers lived in a city where they could go to the office and get the forms; but some of them are living perhaps a hundred miles away from the place where they could get the forms. It is not necessary to have the forms supplied by the board

Unless the forms are supplied by the board the document referred to by my hon. friend would have to be prepared by a legal gentleman and there would be additional cost. Most hon. members who have spoken on this question have expressed a desire to reduce as much as possible
4 p.m. the cost inclined to the soldier.
Unless special forms are prepared by the board stating exactly what is required, these soldiers would have to go to legal men to get the forms prepared, and would have to pay costs. That is not desirable.

My hon. friend has not got the point. I am not talking about the practice or what is going to take place. I am simply speaking in regard to the drafting of the bill. I am in accord with the suggestion of sending out forms to the soldiers, in accord with the principle of preparing a form containing everything that should be in it, and in accord with the principle of having the affidavit set forth everything the soldier has to do and dispensing with any additional written statement. I am suggesting there should not be a statutory requirement that the affidavit should be on a printed form. If the affidavit contained everything set out in the statutory foim, it should be sufficient. It should not be invalidated by reason of the fact that it is not on the statutory form.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I am afraid my hon. friends are raising bogeys that will not exist. If we were going to administer the matter strictly from a legal standpoint and a man v.eie shut out for a technical failure to comply with any of the requirements, it would be a direct endeavour on the part of the government to deny the soldier what is undoubtedly his right, but I think hon. gentlemen will admit that a form duly prepared, with these matters set out in rotation, is the proper thing for the soldiers IMr. Clark}
Did I not say that?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
And due
precaution will be taken to see that he gets them, because there are supervisors in every part of Canada, in every province, and if he does not get them by mail, anyone who makes application by letter or otherwise for such forms will be supplied with them. It will be taken that the letter is an indication of his desire to be dealt with. I do wish my hon. friends would rid their minds of the idea that any soldier will be shut out from consideration because of some legal technicality in the draughtsmanship of the bill.

But the fact is, notwithstanding what the minister says, that the soldier who does not send in his affidavit on a printed form supplied by the department will be debarred. He must comply with this statutory requirement.
No.

That shows how little hon.
gentlemen know about the effect of statutory requirements. The minister suggests that we arc putting up a legal bogey. No more ridiculous suggestion could be made. The principle of the bill having been decided upon, we must necessarily consider the draughtsmanship from the legal standpoint. We do not want the bill draughted by a farmer, and the sooner the minister recognizes as a sound constitutional principle the legal draughtsmanship of this legislation the better it will be for him and his department. I am not raising any bogey at all; I am suggesting something which I trust will facilitate the passage of the bill and at the same time assist not only the department but, as well, the soldier who wants to take advantage of this legislation. The suggestion I make is a. simple one. What possible objection could there be to having the soldier supply a declaration in some .form other than an affidavit if he should happen to lose the printed form supplied him?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Is the hon member arguing against the submission of the printed form proposed?

The minister has missed the point I have raised three times already. I am in perfect accord with the suggestion that the department should prepare a form for submission by the soldier, but I suggest that if by accident the soldier should lose that form a declaration to the same effect be considered valid. That would preclude any possibility of his being shut out from consideration.

Soldier Settlement Act
I do not see why the minister should not accept the hon. member's suggestion. Possibly, however, the man in sending in his own form might forget to dot his i's and cross his Ps.

Does my hon. friend want
to deprive any soldier of any right to which he may be entitled, simply because he happens to send in some other form than that supplied by the department?

No; I do not want to shut
out any soldier.

The difficulty might be met by the use of some such words as these, "that the application shall not be considered invalid by reason of the use of some other form." I do not think any difficulty such as my hon. friend apprehends will actually occur, but the minister might accept this suggestion to set all doubts at rest.

I do not think that in
this particular case an affidavit would be permissible; what is here required is a statutory declaration. My suggestion is that paragraph (b) be amended to read:
The application shall be supported by a statutory declaration setting out the original purchase price of the land.	.
As regards the other requirements as to a written statement and the names and addresses of witnesses, which particulars under the section as it stands are to be supplied on the printed form containing the affidavit, these are matters that could be made the subject of regulation as provided for in paragraph (j). I am sure the minister has misapprehended what my hon. friend (Mr. Clark) has said. There is no tendency whatever on the part of lawyers to be unnecessarily technical, but there is undoubtedly a tendency on the part of members of the committee to assume that when a lawyer makes a suggestion looking to the improvement of a bill he is doing so for the purpose of creating difficulties. That is altogether wrong. 1 would point out to the minister the danger to which the soldier is exposed under the bill as it stands. For example, paragraph (d) provides that all applications for revaluation shall be submitted to the board prior to the first day of October, 1926. Suppose some soldier should fail to send in his application before October 5: that application would be rejected under this provision. We ought, to fix a date late enough to avoid any difficulty of this kind, say November 1. I suggest that the minister amend the section as I propose; a statutory declaration and not an affidavit is what is 14011-160i
here required. Perhaps the Solicitor General will give his opinion on that point.

A statutory declaration or
an affidavit.
The cases in which affidavits are permissible are limited. In the present instance a statutory declaration would be necessary.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Did my hon friend refer to some other part of the section besides paragraph (b) ?
Yes. the written statement as to the value of the land and the names and addresses of witnesses would be a matter of regulation under paragraph (j).

Perhaps the following
draft will meet the views of the committee:
The application shall be supported by a statutory declaration setting forth,
(1) The original purchase price of the land and the value of improvements effected since the establishment of the settler thereon.
2.	His belief as to the present value of the land and his reasons therefor.
3.	The names and addresses of any persons whom the settler proposes as witnesses to the present value.

Certainly; it is the suggestion
I made in the beginning.
Would that be satisfactory?
Certainly.

I think the third is a
most unusual provision. Even on discovery in a civil case, as the Solicitor General (Mr. Cannon) is no doubt aware, the other side is not entitled to get the names of witnesses. Why is it necessary in this case? I submit that it is fundamentally wrong and unjust. I think the settler should put in his application and afterwards appear with his witnesses at the hearing.	.	.

But this is exceptional
procedure and the provision is intended to make the soldier settler show that his claim is serious. As to the regulations which are referred to further on. something might be inserted there to the effect that if any witnesses have been omitted from the original declaration, later they may easily be brought before the board.

That is provided for under the Public Inquiries Act. I suppose, Mr. Chairman, the reason for this is that the man need not come himself; his whole case is given to the board, and the board may call the witnesses he has designated.

speechtext:
It is really
to facilitate his getting his witnesses before the board. However, I have no objection to striking out the paragraph.
No.
If you are preparing a form the notification should be put at the top.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes.

This third subsection apparently leaves it optional with the soldier to supply any names. To my mind this is a very important subsection. I recall when the resolution was before the House a few weeks ago I proposed an additional procedure on the part of the soldier to support his application. I did not get any reply from the minister at that time, and I have been wondering if he heard me. I am of the opinion that a great many soldier settlers are in need of having their land revalued, and every last one who is entitled to it should have this privilege; but I am also of opinion that there are quite a considerable number-and I am thinking of my own constituency when I say this-who are not entitled to a revaluation. There is nothing in this subsection to prevent such men making application for a revaluation. They have simply to give a written statement setting forth their belief as to the value of their land, If a man believes his land will be revalued for $500 or $1,000 less, he is likely to stretch his belief a long way. I have suggested, and I again suggest, that the application of the soldier settler should be supported by a resolution, duly moved and passed by the local municipal council. I should like to hear if the minister has any objection to the addition of a fourth subsection reading somewhat as follows:
4.	By a written statement of the local municipal council setting forth their belief as to (the present value and their reasons therefor.
I make this proposal because the municipal councillors know the land and know the settler and are in a better position to give a fair and impartial view than he is himself.
Before the minister considers that suggestion, let me point out that it would not work at all in British Columbia.
Hear, hear.

That part of the province
which is municipalized is very small, and a very large proportion of the soldiers are in the absolutely unorganized districts.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I agree with my hon. friend from Kindersley (Mr. Carmichael) that one undoubtedly would get refMr. Geary.]
liable information from a municipal council. Perhaps no body of men know their locality better than they do. But the adoption of his suggestion would entail the expense of notifying them, and I think he will agree with me that if the local council reported against any revaluation they would be in a rather awkward position, and the soldier would have an everlasting grievance. That is one of the reasons why I felt it necessary to extend the privilege of revaluation to every soldier whether entitled to consideration or not. Our hope is that we will settle this once for all, giving every man a full opportunity to make has statement, and then the board will either agree or disagree with it. Naturally, in dealing with it they would seek their information from the very body that my hon. friend has mentioned.

Shall the subsection carry?

It was not intended by the minister originally that the whole statement of the settler setting forth his belief as to the present value of his land and the reasons therefor should be under oath. Why is it necessary to go further now and have all the material under oath?

The amendment was suggested by the hon. member for West Calgary (Mr. Bennett) and the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens). In order to simplify matters this amendment is proposed. Under it there would be only one document, which would contain the particulars enumerated in the clause as it read originally. I do not think there is any serious suggestion that the settler should in a statutory declaration state his reason for a revaluation. If he is serious he will have no objection to putting that in a declaration.
It should all be under oath.

That is my opinion.

Would the Solicitor
General agree to the addition of a provision at the end of the amendment to the effect that the settler may call witnesses who are not included in that list?
In order not to complicate the clause I think my hon. friend should refer to clause (j) on page 3. The regulations, which are to be made by the Governor in Council, could cover these cases.
Very well, if that is understood.
What regulations are those?

If we did that we might
work a hardship on the soldier.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I am quite prepared to strike that out, because I anticipate that we will have trouble when the regulations come up.

I would like to support that. I do not want to make a speech again, but I feel it my duty to support what has been said about the names and addresses of the witnesses There, is no earthly reason for that. It is a very unusual thing; no man is supposed to disclose the names and addresses of his witnesses. Another and more serious objection is this: Is it really proposed that when this list is given and the matter is heard, the settler cannot call anyone else? If we are to have an amendment at all why not get rid of the whole thing, and set out the three things originally proposed, the original price of the land; the value of improvements and the present value of the land. I am going to make this suggestion, that those three items be given, and verified by affidavit.
Under the amendment proposed by the Solicitor General there must be a statutory declaration, and it cannot be done otherwise.

I have no objection to
striking out the last part of my amendment, that is,
The names and addresses of any persons whom the settler proposes as witnesses to the present vaiue.

Paragraph (b) as amended agreed to.
On paragraph (c)-How depreciation shall be computed:

I would like to ask the minister why the improvements are included. I understood that this was a revaluation of land, and I also understood that there had been a rebate allowed in respect of improvements. Why are the two linked together now?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Does my
hon. friend mean that there has already been a rebate for improvements?
I am not sure whether there was really a rebate, but there was a bill before the House to that effect.

I take it that the improvements referred to would be part of the land. They are the fences, the wells, the breaking, the clearing and the houses, and when they are sold to the settler they are sold as part of the land. They are only distinguished from the land for the purposes of the land titles acts of some of the provinces. When you sell so many acres of land, with so much broken, so much cleared, so much fencing done, a well, a residence, a barn and so on, they become part of the land and are sold with it. Therefore if you leave out the words " and the improvements " you will cover everything.
It means the improvements sold to the settler.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I am given to understand that the old act makes that definition. I quite agree with my hon. friend that the improvements are included with the land, but apparently those words were inserted to meet an objection raised in committee. In one case we might have a man who, by his action, had reduced the value of the land, while on the other hand his neighbour, by industry, had improved the value of the land by adding permanent improvements. It was to meet that objection which was raised in committee that these words were inserted, so that the settler would receive consideration for the improvements made while he occupied the land.
Soldier Settlement Act

Still I do not see the point, because when the soldier buys land he buys it with so much clearing, so much breaking, so much fencing, so many buldings and so on, -and he buys it as land. For the sake of convenience a distinction was made between land and improvements, but he bought it as a farm, as land. If, when you come to revalue that, you take the difference between the value of the land you sold him, the price at which it was sold, and the present value of the land, you will get the same thing.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I may say that I argued in the same way, but I did not convince the committee that that man would be taken care of.

I agree with the hon. member for East Edmonton (Mr. Bury) on the legal principle, but supposing a man buys unimproved land for 83,000. He then puts improvements on the land to the value of 81,500, and they become part of the land. They are called improvements, but they are really a part of the land, which makes a total value of $4,500. In other words, he has added $1,500 to the value of his property by his own effort. He is of opinion that the land has depreciated in value by fifty per cent. His land is therefore worth $1,500, but assuming that the improvements have not depreciated in value, the total value of his property will be to-day exactly what it was when he acquired it, namely, $3,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: That is exactly what we cover in this subsection.
Is that man entitled to a revaluation? Is he entitled to any consideration for the depreciation in land value, apart from his improvements?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes.
I confess that I cannot see at the moment just where that is provided for in this act.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I thought we were providing for that contingency; we made it very clear in the former drafts that improvements made by the settler would be taken into consideration. This covers the point just raised by my hon. friend. In that case the idea would be to give the settler full credit for the improvements placed upon the land by himself; the valuation would be made quite apart from those improvements, and a reduction made in accordance with that valuation.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The amendment was introduced to cover exactly the cases cited by both hon. gentlemen, that is, where permanent improvements had been made, which, after all, apply to the land itself. I agree with my hon. friend that we had that covered, but in order to satisfy the committee we added those words, and every ease of that kind will be considered on its merits. The value that was contributed to the property by the soldier himself will be given consideration and not be included in the reduction in valuation, if any,-of the property.

I do not like to speak so
often but this is an important matter. What I am going to suggest to the minister is this: There are apparently now to be considered two factors in valuing the property which the settler purchased-the factor of the raw land, and the factor of the improvements worked into or put upon that raw land. When you come to revalue, I think you will have to revalue those two factors separately. I think you will have to take into account this question:	Has the value of raw land in this district gone down as raw land? If it has, the settler must be compensated or get a concession in respect of the reduction in the value of the raw land in that district. Then take 'the second factor, the improvements that he purchased at the time. He may have allowed those improvements to go down, or he may have added to them. For that reason I think you will have to keep these two factors separate-the factor of the raw land, and the factor of the improvement. In the revaluation you will have to ask yourself: what was the value of the raw land when that man purchased? One thousand dollars; the value of that raw land now is eight hundred dollars Very well then; the farm in respect of that factor has depreciated two hundred dollars. Then take the other factor, the improvements. What was the value of the improvements at the time he purchased? One thousand or fifteen hundred dollars. What is the value of the improvements now? It has gone up.

Soldier Settlement Act
Very well then, we need not bother in that ease. The value has gone down; then we must take into account the depreciation of the improvements. I do no<t know whether I have made myself clear, but I do not think you will settle this question until you keep those two factors separate and have a revaluation of the two factors.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I think it
is quite unnecessary that we should go into that detail in the bill, but undoubtedly that would have to be the basis on which the revaluation would be made, because there are the two factors here. We wanted to make it perfectly clear that if the soldier by his own labour and industry had improved the value of the property, he should be given consideration for that improvement.

But this section does not
do that. As this section reads, if a man buys land and improvements through the Soldier Settlement Board, and adds to those improvements by building a barn or an addition 'to his house, 'he will not receive credit for those improvements under the section as drafted. They will be added to the present value of the land, and if the present value of the land with these improvements that have been made by the soldier himself equals the price which he paid for .the farm originality, he will not be entitled to any revaluation.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
My hon.
friend is hardly correct there. Take the concrete case he mentions, where the soldier adds a bam to the land and improvements that were sold to him at a fixed price, and he makes that improvement by his own industry or with money he has procured. Of necessity that improvement adds to the value of that particular farm. It may have depreciated from the day he built it, but the present day value of that improvement would be credited to 'him, and would not be taken into consideration in fixing the depreciation of the property. We are endeavouring to give credit for the improvements the settler puts in, for the improvements which were not made by the government, and which were not in existence when the settler took possession of the property. It is a little bit complicated, but that is the clear intention of what we are endeavouring to do here.

I think we are all in accord as to what is desired here, but possibly there is some room for doubt as to whether that will be accomplished by the wording as it stands, and if there is any doubt, I would like to suggest to the minister that he add in the

We know that in regard to other matters demands have come from various public bodies for uniform legislation. Here we have a bill in regard to old age pensions which is likely to bring about uniformity. It is quite true that the provinces cannot be forced into enacting legislation, but no one is trying to do that in connection with this matter. All we are doing here is passing an act which will be very advantageous to the people of Canada if it is adopted generally.

With respect to the remarks of my hon. friend (Mr. Heaps) what objection could there be to any of the provinces making a larger contribution towards old age pensions than is provided for in this bill if they so desire? For example, British Columbia might consider that the allowance should be larger. There would be some argument in favour of that, because $20 a month will not even meet the cost of keeping an old person in one of the provincial old people's homes.
Is there anything in the bill to prevent the amount being increased? There must be a certain minimum, but I do not think there is any provision against increasing the grant.
Yes, but the minister says he wants to have uniformity, in which case we must have the same allowance in every province.

It is quite true that the section we are discussing provides that no change be made in the scheme by a province without the consent of the Governor in Council. The bill is based on the understanding that the Dominion government will contribute $10 out of the $20 that goes to each pensioner, but I think the idea is that this amount shall be the minimum. The**, is nothing to prevent any provincial government, as I read the bill, from increasing the amount of its grant by $5 or $10. I hope some of the provinces will do so. The federal government would hardly raise any opposition to their taking that course.
Should any province desire to increase its contribution I do not think there is any question about the Dominion government agreeing to it.
Then what the minister meant was a uniform minimum contribution? May I ask the minister what provinces have intimated that they agree with this legislation?

As a matter of fact section 9 of the bill fixes $240 as the maximum. I do not think the question of the provinces contributing a larger amount has been considered. At any rate it is not dealt with in this legislation. At present we are engaged in drafting a bill which we hope will be acceptable to the provinces, and the question as to what should be done in the event of the provinces wanting to increase their contribution may properly be a subject of future discussion.
The minister did not answer my question; perhaps he did not hear it. I asked how many of the provinces have intimated that they will contribute towards this scheme.

I suggest that we would make better progress if we confined our discussion to the clause under consideration. I do not know whether my hon. friend was present yesterday, but the subject of the correspondence which had taken place with the various provincial governments came up and was fully discussed. If my hon. friend wants information on that subject he will find it in the report of the parliamentary committee. If he has not a copy at hand I will send one over to him.

On this section I wish to
reiterate the position I took when the reso-
Old Age Pensions

lution on which this bill is founded was under discussion. This section shows quite clearly that it is foolish to try to force this bill through until an attempt has been made to get uniformity of action on the part of the provinces. We are all agreed as to the necessity of an old age pension scheme; any argument on that is merely wasting time. We are all agreed as to the necessity of uniformity of legislation, and any argument on that also is wasting time. It is entirely a question of how best to attain uniformity. I wish again to state my view that you will never get uniformity until you have got the provinces together and found out how far they are prepared to go. The very question of contribution or non-contribution lies at the whole root of the possibility of uniformity. The first thing the government ought to do is to call a conference of provincial representatives and ascertain whether they are willing to come in on the one scheme or the other, on a contributory scheme or on a noncontributory scheme. Let that be settled first. Until we get this expression of uniformity from the provinces we do not know where we are. Yesterday when this matter was being discussed, the Prime Minister said the reason why he wished this bill to go through was, that he might have something to submit to the premiers of the different provinces. Unless you have a concrete set of proposals to submit to the provinces when you call them together, it will be almost impossible to get anywhere. There is no reason in the world why the Prime Minister should not draft his scheme as he conceives it should be. submit a bill-this bill, if you like, as it now stands-to the representatives of the provinces, get them to discuss it, and as soon as they have discussed it come back to parliament and submit to parliament the bill as agreed on by the provinces. I say again that by adopting the present method you are inviting the provinces to make the retort that they should have been consulted in the first instance.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
When the committee
rose shortly before six o'clock, section 5 was under consideration. Shall the section carry?

The committee had discussed the section at some length, and I gathered that the minister hoped later on to enlighten us further on the question it involved. Is he in a position now to answer some of the questions brought to his attention?

I cannot agree
with hon. gentlemen opposite who think that this legislation wTill be ineffective and will fail to make for uniformity. I believe that uniform legislation throughout Canada will follow the enactment of this bill.

I have not before spoken
on the principle of the bill, having taken it for granted from the very outset that inasmuch as advanced legislation in the matter of old age pensions had been adopted in all of the leading countries in the world a similar measure if introduced in this parliament would meet with general approval. Some question has been raised by certain remarks made by the Premier of Quebec, but I am of the opinion that, when this bill goes through, not only the premier of that province but the legislature and the people of Quebec generally will be prepared to give it full consideration.
Considerable emphasis has been laid on the suggestion that this legislation is likely to be of most value in the cities in assisting the working classes. I dissent from that opinion; I think the provisions of the bill will be most beneficial in the outlying districts. In the province of Quebec we have large institutions in the cities to take care of the -aged, while there are no such places in the outlying parts of the country, and it is in these places that this old age pension scheme will be most appreciated. I am satisfied that the bill when it passes will receive the careful consideration as well as the support of the province of Quebec, and for that reason among others I am glad that the government is persisting in putting it through the House.

In this matter, as in
several others which this government has

Old Age Pensions
undertaken, I believe we are beginning wrong. The government should 'have approached the various provinces and ascertained their views before introducing the legislation we are now considering, for it i3 manifest that the bill can be of no value unless advantage is taken of it in the provinces. For that reason the opinions of the various premiers should have been consulted. The hon. member (Mr. Marcil) believes that in the province of Quebec legislation of this kind would be most effective in rural communities. In Ontario, I may tell him, we have in a great majority of the counties 'homes for aged people kept at the expense of the province, and these homes, I fancy, will be more or less affected by this legislation. I think the legislation should have been preceded by a conference of the government with the provinces.

The Object of this bill is dear to my heart, as it has always been, but the scheme in its details does not approach my ideal of an old age pensions law. In the older parts of Canada the provinces have always provided very well for those who are unable to support themselves. In my own province there is an estimable system of caring for the aged, and for the young as well when these are unable to take care of themselves. We have county homes there. Formerly they were called poor houses and the people who lived in them were known to the public as paupers. Happily the condition suggested by these names no longer exists; we are more enlightened to-day and we have very good institutions which are described by the less disagreeable name of county homes. The inmates are well treated and have a home where everything is provided for them. They are not obliged to work, but they can enjoy themselves at gardening and so forth, and the product of their labour is always at their disposal. While that may not be the intention of this bill, it is not to my mind doing very much better. Twenty dollars a month will not go very far in providing for an aged couple, for I gather that only the husband would be entitled to a pension. I may be wrong, I hope I am, but if only twenty dollars a month is available, how far will that provide the necessaries of decent living for a couple both over seventy years of age? In the institutions in my province with which I am acquainted it costs $5 to $5.50 a week to provide for each inmate, and this does not take into account anything for rent or Shelter. That is one fault I have to find with the bill- the pension is insufficient.
A still greater defect in my opinion is that we are seeking to impose on the provinces 14011-161
something without knowing whether or not they are in favour of it. In fact, it seems to me to be an attempt to interfere with provincial rights. Above all else, it is of vital importance to cultivate a spirit of harmony in the relations between the federal government and the various provincial governments. If the bill was based on the mortuary tables and the contributory principle adopted to the extent of a half or a quarter of the amount of the pension, the government providing the balance, then I think we would have a scheme that the people would be proud of, and no one availing himself of its provisions would feel that he was being spoon-fed. The government might establish such a scheme on a fair basis by a vote of one or two hundred thousand dollars, or more if necessary. I would make the terms very lenient to those who might fall behind with their payments so that it would be possible for them to clear off their arrears as opportunity offered. But before we can be assured of any success with this bill we will have to secure the co-operation of the provincial governments. I have no authority officially to say so, but it seems to me-and my impressions, of course are gathered from the daily press-that it is not reasonable to suppose that the government of my province will be prepared to undertake new7 liabilities at the present time. Our province is just recovering from a splurge of bad government, so bad, indeed, that w7e are obliged to resort to direct taxation, something we never imagined would ever be necessary. I hope the federal government will hold their hand until such time as they have secured the co-operation of the provincial governments in this proposal.

Mr. Chairman, it is very
gratifying to those who are interested in the welfare of humanity to find such splendid sentiments expressed here in regard to this bill It does seem to me, however, that there is a tendency to say to our less fortunate brothers, be warmed and fed, and yet not give them those things which are needed. In a scheme that has to be worked out by the Dominion in conjunction with the provinces, necessarily some difficulties are involved in making a start. Now, if we held a conference with tlhe provinces we would probably find a great deal of difficulty in getting unanimity of opinion among them, and no start would be made. Here are two parties to the contract, the Dominion on the one hand and a group of provinces on the other. One party or the other has to make a start, and in my judgment the quickest way to secure unanimity of opinion in the matter is to pass this bill.

Old Age Pensions

I do not think any province would fail to pass the necessary implementing legislation if this House clearly put itself on record as being in favour of tihe principle of the bill, and instead of merely giving utterance to a lot of pious wishes, translated' those wishes into something concrete. I repeat, I am firmly convinced that the quickest way to secure action is for parliament to pass this bill.
New, a good deal has been said somewhat wide of the mark respecting the relative merits of a contributory or a non-contributory scheme. I am heartily in sympathy with any move calculated to encourage thrift among our people, and 1 should like to see the provisions made for annuities brought more forcibly to their attention; but it seems to me that we will have simply to follow the course that has been fallowed in other countries. In England the pension scheme began in a non-contributor y form. In my judgment it is the only way it can be introduced, and I fully anticipate that if this non-contributory scheme is launched, within a very short time we will find ourselves entering upon a contributory scheme. That is the natural evolution of any pension legislation; I do not see how it can be otherwise. We cannot take care of the immediate necessities by any contributory scheme tlhat can be mentioned, but in course of time that can be built up, and in the meantime we will have a measure such as is now proposed that will be taking care of the immediate requirements of our aged poor. So I do not think we need be alarmed because some person points to England and says: They began in such-and-such a way, and they were compelled to do so-and-so at a later day. It seems to me that that is only what we may expect. Mr. Chairman, I feel thoroughly convinced that if we are to get action at all the onl;' way is for that body which can act as a unit to put its concrete proposal before the provinces.

The hon. member for Lisgar (Mr. Brown) is rather inconsistent, for in one breath he says we want something positive, and in the next he says we should put through this bill. There is nothing positive about this bill; on the contrary, it is very uncertain indeed and depends upon receiving the approval of the provincial legislatures. I submit that if there is a responsibility upon this House to do something positive, we should pass a bill to establish old age pensions. If we want to do that, but think the total obligation involved is too much for the country to shoulder at the present time, although it is very prosperous according to the statement of the Minister of

Finance, then we might divide it up. We admit our responsibility of $10 a month; we are prepared to give that amount provided the provinces do likewise, but if the provinces do not contribute the old people will not. receive anything at all. If we admit our responsibility for $10 a month should we not put through a positive bill and provide for the payment of at least that amount fo the aged in any event? I submit that that should be taken into consideration, as well as the further question whether or not this parliament should undertake the whole responsibility of $20 a month.

Mr. Chairman, I just
want to say a word about this bill.
On a point of order, Mr. Chairman; are we not considering clause 5 of the bill.

speechtext: I do not want to compel hon. members to speak exactly to the clause; they should keep as close to it as possible. I had not started when the hon. member for North Winnipeg (Mr. Heaps) presumed to take the lead of this House. In opening, I would like to put myself on record as being in favour of civilized countries looking after their aged poor, but I want to bring to the attention of the committee one or two points in connection with this matter. We are a young country; we have to-day resources greater than many other countries; we have the largest amount of agricultural land per capita; we have the greatest mines, the greatest forests, the greatest natural resources-and we have a population of about nine million people. Are we prepared at present to put eveiyone on the pay roll of the country? It seems to m* that we are getting the habit in this parlia' ment of going-I was going to say " mad "-iv. the way of legislation.
We have not pissed any as yet.

We have not passed any, but we have a certain clique, of which the hon. member is one, which desires to fasten every responsibility, whether municipal or

provincial, on the Dominion treasury. This government should either have enough courage to say, " We are going to have an old age pension scheme, and we will take the responsibility of putting through the legislation and of bearing the financial burden," or else this bill should not have been introduced i'-t all.
What is going to be the result? The government are trying to fasten this responsibility upon the provinces, without having consulted them. Presuming that this bill passes, what will be the result if the provinces do not agree to it? Supposing a province does agree for a few years and then, after getting a number of people on the pension list, sees fit to withdraw from the scheme; where is the responsibility to rest? What is this government going to do? I asked the Prime Minister last night if he was willing to take the responsibility of establishing a scheme of old age pensions, with the Dominion, bearing the financial responsibility, and he said no. Is this a scheme to assist the establishment of old age pensions or is it not? The Prime Minister has not as yet answered that question, a question which should be answered before proceeding with this legislation.
The hon. member for Fort William (Mr. Manion) read last night the answers received from every province, and without a single exception they did not agree to this legislation. I would like to ask the minister what he is going to do if the provinces continue to disagree. What then will be the object of this legislation?

To secure the votes of
a couple of members.

I quite agree; it is a
political scheme to get votes in this parliament, and nothing else. I ask the Prime Minister again whether he, as the head of this government, is willing to take the responsibility of introducing an old age pension scheme into this parliament and of bearing the financial responsibility for such a scheme.
