At the risk of being
tedious I again call the attention of the government to the fact enunciated by the hon. member for Fort William, namely, that none of the provinces have agreed to this legislation. I further call the attention of the Minister of Public Works, under whose direction this bill is introduced, to the fact that in many of the provinces, particularly in Ontario, we already have a scheme for the care of the aged. Apparently no effort has been made by this government to ascertain the opinion of Ontario, or that of any other province which has a similar scheme; or if any such attempt has been made the reply has not been in favour of the principle of this bill. As pointed out by the hon. member for Muskoka, even if a province did accept the principle of this bill for a time but withdrew from it later, the Dominion government would be in a quandary. I think we are perfectly right in stating that our position should be either yes or no. Are we in favour of old age pensions or are we not?
We are.

The hon. member for
North Winnipeg says we are; then we should assume the whole responsibility and the Dominion of Canada should be responsible for the entire financial burden. Why divide it up in this way; why pass a bill of this kind when we know that most of the provinces will not assent to it as it is now before parliament?
We do not know that; the hon. member is guessing. .

We know it by inference; the provinces have not accepted the principle so far, and the probability is that they will not accept it, Even if it is accepted, there is nothing which would compel them to continue in that acceptance. We are starting at the wrong end, as I said before. Let the government say, "We are prepared to put through a measure of old age pensions," or "We are trying to shove the responsibility on someone else."

It would be a mistake to shut off debate on this bill, because as the debate goes on members are appreciating more and more the importance of old age pensions, and we see that if in the future we have to introduce a scheme of this kind under which the Dominion government must take full responsibility, we will receive support from those whom we thought, at the
Old Age Pensions

beginning of the debate, were against such a measure. At the beginning of this debate I recall that there were some members on the other side of the House who took the position that the country could not stand this expenditure, but now they contend that we are not spending enough, and that we ought to give another twelve million dollars towards old age pensions. So I think the longer we discuss this subject the better we shall get along.
It seems to me, Mr. Chairman, that if we are really sincere in trying to put an old age pension bill through, instead of arousing antagonism on the part of the provinces by speeches here to the effect that we are attempting to force something on them, if this bill is satisfactory in other respects- as to the amount of pension payable, and the conditions upon which it shall be granted-[DOT] we ought to get together and pass it and leave it to the provinces either to accept or reject it. The provincial governments are composed of men of sound business ability, men who wish to do the right thing by their province, although I find that even the Premier of Ontario has been trying to make a little political capital in connection with this matter. Not so very long ago he was asked on the floor of the Ontario legislature if he was considering an old age pension scheme for Ontario, and he said yes: that is, Ontario was considering an old age pension scheme for that province. But after there had been a certain amount of debate on this scheme in this House and the Premier of Ontario saw that some members on the Conservative side were opposed to it, he made the statement to the effect that the old age pension'for Ontario, if it was to be given in co-operation with the Dominion government according to the terms of this bill, would be too expensive. In other words, he was considering an old age pension plan for Ontario whereby Ontario would have borne the whole cost of an old age pension for that province; yet when the Dominion government proposed to pay fifty per cent of the cost, he said that this scheme would be too expensive.
I noticed in the Free Press the other day a quotation from the Vancouver Province, and the Free Press went on to say that here was the Dominion government introducing a bill that was nothing more than a sop.
Hear, hear.

If the Ontario government, justly as the hon. member claims, and as I believe, put into force the mothers' allowance, why should they not take care of their aged in the same way? Or if the Dominion government is disposed to pay fifty per cent towards the cost of this pension for those of our population who are not able to sustain themselves after seventy, why should not the Dominion government also pay fifty per cent towards the cost of the mothers' allowance?

I am glad my hon. friend has asked that question, because I was coming to that. But let us look at this thing in a practical way, and not have any hypothetical questions or indulge in imaginations regarding it. Let us see how it will work out in practice. The provinces are now responsible for the maintenance of their aged people who are not able to take care of themselves,and how do they look after them? By putting them in houses of refuge or poorhouses, where in many cases an old couple will be separated from each other. Is that the proper way to look after our old people?

They do not do it that
way.

There are some people who do not know everything in this world, and I am speaking to one of them now. The Labour men of this country have been to the provincial government as well as to the federal government asking that an old age
pension scheme be put into effect, and some of the provinces have said that it would be too great a burden upon them and they could not do it, that it was the Dominion's duty. In other words, we have been passing the buck for a great many years on this question. In former days when the Dominion government or the provincial government were asked to shoulder the responsibility for such legislation none of them wanted to do it.
Mr. ARTHL'RS:	And this government
does not want to do it now.

You do not know; you
only think that. Now, the present Dominion government say this to the provinces:	We
know you have a burden on your shoulders at the present time in caring for these people. In order to bring about an old age pension we are going to lay down certain conditions and if you accept those conditions it will be possible for us to do something. I think the conditions laid down are fair because they have been investigated and recommended by a committee of this House, a committee composed of representatives of all parties. I am quite sure that the members of the provincial legislatures are just as reasonable as the members of this House, and they will be prepared to do what is right. The Labour people have discussed this matter and have made certain recommendations. The present bill, I think, carries out the recommendations of the parliamentary committee, almost to the letter. Very well; the Dominion government said to the provinces:	We will provide machinery
and we will contribute fifty per cent of the amount needed in order to help you to maintain aged people. As to the amount of pension, if an amendment were moved to increase the amount from $240 to $300 I would be willing to support something along that line, but if this House agrees upon the amount mentioned as reasonable, why not let us get together and put the law into effect? Instead of trying to suggest what the Senate may do with the bill, or to antagonize the provinces or to see who can get the most political prestige out of it, why not let us get together, make the very best arrangements we can, and then say "This is the very best we can give for the present and encourage the provinces to take advantage of it."
Why does the hon. member say "this is the best we can give"? In saying that does he speak for the Minister of Labour, or for himself?

I was speaking of all of
us as members of the House, including my hon. friend.

It was not my intention to take part in this diseussion, but the remarks of the hon. member for Muskoka (Mr. McGibbon) tempted me to get on my feet for a few moments. . I heartily approve of the principle of this bill, and I think this measure is long overdue. Those of us who have had the opportunity on many occasions to meet old people in our professional work must surely recognize the fact that there are many cases of parents who have given sons and daughters in great number to this country but who, through some misfortune have found themselves in the latter years of their lives dependent upon charity. I am quite sure that my hon. friend (Mr. McGibbon) as well as the other medical men in this House, have met cases of that kind. That being so, why Should any medical man oppose a bill which will bring relief and comfort to aged men and 'women who deserve so well of their country?

Does the hon. member
think for a moment that any man is going to get relief from this bill? I am opposing it because I know they will not.

My hon. friend made an observation towards the close of his speech to the effect that this legislation was intended for political effect.	That is what
I take great exception to.	I invite hon.
gentlemen opposite to join for once the rest of the members of this House in putting through one bill of a humanitarian character. Let us unite in such a good work and if any political advantage is to be gained at all, let us all share in it.

May I ask my hon.
friend another question?
Certainly.
I ask him as a gentleman, and I know he is one, to be accurate when he quotes me. I made no such statement.

Well, if the hon. gentleman did not mention "the political effect" of this bill, my ears deceived me. Certainly he said a moment ago that he does not think any man will get relief from the bill. I quite agree with the hon. member for Lisgar (Mr. Brown) that if we pass this bill and make a certain amount of money available for the desired purpose there will not be one province in Canada that will not take advantage of it. It will only be a very short time until all the provinces will be availing themselves of this legislation and then the aged people who come under its provisions

will be getting some help in their declining years. It is a lamentable thing to see old men and women in receipt of charity. If this bill passes they will not be in receipt of charity; no such stigma will be attached to the enjoyment of the pension granted under this bill. If we pass this measure we shall all have occasion to feel proud of ourselves; for by the enactment of a bill based on such humanitarian principles this parliament will have done something greatly to its credit.

Mr. Chairman, I was just going to call your attention to this fact: We have been waiting for an approach to a consideration of some of the sections of the bill because we have certain suggestions to make. My hon. friend opposite, and particularly the last two speakers, while professing to talk on the principle of the bill, have been introducing some rather sharp criticisms of our position. We certainly have suggestions to make with respect to this bill and we propose to make them; but I submit that the best way for the government to make progress with the measure is to ask their own supporters to keep within the bounds of specific clauses so that whatever discussion takes place may have some point and some effect. I am giving notice to the government now that with respect to some of the clauses we are approaching I have suggestions to make which I hope will be constructive and useful; but if we go on with a general, desultory discussion of this character for two or three hours it will not assist us to rush through all the sections without discussion at all. We may as well approach the real matter of these sections as carry on a discussion of the kind which has taken place for the last three-quarters of an hour. I make these statements as I do not wish to be charged later on in the evening with obstructing the bill.

I do not know whether
the draughting of this bill is very important or not. It may be, but I question whether it is worth a very detailed examination. I do not apprehend that the bill is going to come into effect until we will have had a lot more opportunity to review it. But if it is, I must say that to me it is a masterpiece of draughting. Take this section, for example. The criticism I have to make here is not as serious as I think can be made with respect to some other features of the bill. The main feature of the bill from this point of view is that it is principally an authority to pass an act. It is not an act. If hon. gentlemen will look at section 19-

We have not
reached that section yet.

But in order to speak
of the draughting I have to mention it. Look at the length of that section and the authority it gives to the Governor in Council as to regulations. The bill is going to be drafted under that section, some time, somewhere, by someone. The whole alphabet, or almost the whole alphabet, was exhausted in the mere enumeration of the sections which the Governor in Council uses for the purposes of draughting the bill, and the matters referred to there are the very sum and substance, the very life and fibre, of the whole thing. Nobody knows what in the world this bill is going to be. I suppose the government knows as little as anybody else, but it is going to be draughted under clause 19, if it is ever draughted at all. Section 5 says:
Before any agreement made pursuant to this aot co-mes into operation the Governor in Council shall approve the scheme for the administration of pensions pro-posed to be adopted by the province, and no change in such scheme shall be made by the province without the consent of the Governor in Council.
In draughtsmanship, what is a " scheme " and especially a scheme for the administration of an act? I understand the purpose of the draughtsman is to make the provincial act subject to the approval of the Governor in Council. If that is the purpose it should say so, and not say " the scheme for the administration of pensions proposed to be adopted by the province." Who is going to tell what part of the act is included in this scheme for the administration of pensions? Is the provincial authority to decide, or is it the federal authority? I have an idea what the draughtsman wants to say, but he has not said it. In the next clause the same word comes in. I have never seen before in the phraseology of any statute a " scheme " to provide for the organization. It seems to me to be far simpler and better to say the provincial act shall be subject to the approval of the Governor in Council.
Hon. members have said-and I was almost moved to tears by the eloquence of the hon. member for Saskatoon (Mr. Young) on this subject-that the great object of this movement is to relieve the aged and the distressed, to remove them from the shadow of the poor-house, and to take care of them in their old age in a manner consistent with their dignity and in a way which comports with what old age really demands. I cannot see how anybody is going to come out of the poorhouse under this bill, if it ever goes into effect. Who can come out of the poorhouse on $240 a year? If I were arguing that we ought to set
to work to get everybody out of the poorhouse, I would say we should have a bill that would do it. This bill will not do it. I am not arguing however, for that purpose; I am simply saying that those who think this is a plan to bring that about have only to read the clauses of the bill. If one looks ahead he will see that the Governor in Council is going to be able, under the regulations, to provide that the provinces pay their share to the workhouse. That is how they will do it. How else can they do it when they only pay half? There is no other way. All we are going to achieve by this bill is to help the provinces keep up the poorhouses, assuming the provinces come into the scheme. Is that an unfair statement of the result?
Is that the position in the other countries where old age pensions are in effect?
I do not know. This is a federation, the other countries are not a federation.

Australia was somewhat in
the same category.

No; and anyway if we provided a larger amount-although I am not arguing for it-there would be some hope of taking the old people out of the poorhouse and putting them in their homes. But when we confine it to this proposition it is pure hypocrisy on our part to throw out the signal to the aged people of Canada that the shadow of the poorhouse is no more about them and that we are going to keep them comfortably in their homes. Can the hon. member for North Winnipeg suggest any way on earth by which an old person can live on $240 a year?

If there are two old people will they not receive $40 a month? One old person would not care to live alone, and if they lived together, one perhaps as a paying guest, I think they could be taken care of on this amount.

If it was a case of man and wife they might, but I doubt if it would be possible even then; they would require to have their health and be able to look after themselves. But there is the difficulty with old age; old people cannot look after themselves, consequently it is the home that looks after them. If they have their health and are able to look after themselves, a man and his wife might live on $480 a year, but I do not know. Erom what I have seen of efforts to do it I would rather see them living in a comfortable home such as they have in Portage la Prairie.

Would my right hon. friend refuse to give them anything at all because he could not give them everything they want?

No, that is not the point I am malting at all. There may be places where the provinces and municipalities- and those are terms we can use synonymously here, for one is under the other-might be able to take care of them in some way and keep them comfortably. If there are, I do not know where to find them. I am not denying that there may be some, but I know it would not be in Manitoba. I know something about the home there. I do not say there is not something, of course, in the nature of humiliation in going to what we call a home, but it is not a penal institution. There are hundreds of men in these places, and no person could live more comfortably than they do there, though they might live more luxuriously; but the home is open to all. I venture to say that of all the occupants of that home there are very few who are man and wife. There might be some, but I never ran across such a case; they are nearly all old single people, old brothers, or something of that sort. You cannot for the sum of $240 maintain these people elsewhere with anything like the comfort by which they are surrounded there. It may be wise for us to come to the relief of the provinces-although I do not know that we have been asked to do so-in order to elevate the standard of these places. I do not think very many members of the House would feel reluctant about endorsing such a proposition. There may be places where the standard is not as high as that with whidi I am acquainted in Manitoba; it is probably lower in other places. I would like to see the standard raised everywhere, and I think the provinces can well afford it. But when we are talking in this committee about getting rid of the poorhouses, as we would like to get rid of the gaols, we are only raising a hope soon to be shattered, because we cannot do it by means of this measure.
The hon. member for Lisgar says we must go through the same process as others have done who were in the field earlier than we were. There have been other countries in the field earlier than we, but hon. gentlemen must remember that great indus-9 p.m. trial countries necessarily reach this stage sooner than a country like Canada or the United States. If they learn by experience, by what process of reasoning does it follow we must commit all their errors to get the Same experience? I would

like to hear the argument behind that contention. It is said that you have got to start without contribution. Why? Must we start without contribution because we cannot make those over seventy years of age contribute? Is that any reason why those under seventy need not do so? None whatever. In a word, if we are ever to start the contributory principle it is never going to be as easy to do it as it is now-certainly it never will be easier. Any difficulties in our way now will certainly be in our way when we think of commencing again. It is true you cannot start with those who are called pensioners under this act, but you can make a start with prospective pensioners, and give everybody the right to come in and earn; and you may have the system graded according to age. There would be no difficulty whatever, in carrying out such a proposal. These are simply suggestions I offer touching the details of the measure. My opinion on the measure in genera! was offered to the House last night for whatever it was worth.

I agree with the suggestion
of the hon. member (Mr. Stevens) that we confine ourselves to the section under discussion; we are now considering section 5, which has nothing to do with a contributory scheme. That will come under another section and in my opinion consideration of it might very well be deferred.

Section 5 provides that before any agreement made pursuant to this legislation becomes operative the Governor General shall approve the scheme for the administration of pensions proposed to be adopted by the province. The first three words of this paragraph presuppose an agreement with a province or with provinces of the Dominion. Now, it is possible that some ideas which may occur to one in connection with this section might more properly have been stated when the resolution on which this bill was founded was under consideration, but I venture to think that the word "agreement" here will warrant the views I have to offer. At the present moment I can see no possibility of Nova Scotia entering into an agreement with the Dominion government on a fifty-fifty basis of contribution to a scheme of this kind. Even taking the sum mentioned of $240 a year and assuming the aggregate contribution to be evenly distributed over the provinces, it would call for practically one million dollars to meet the pensions required in Nova Scotia. So that if that province were forced to raise its share of $500,000 towards the provincial contribution it would mean that my own

Old Age Pensions
constituency, as one of the fourteen which would be taxed in the province, would have to provide something like $35,000 in addition to what we are already paying to take care of the poor people of Nova Scotia.
I want to aseure the committee that the poor of the province are being reasonably well taken care of at present. If Nova Scotia does not participate in this scheme, and if only one province in the Dominion takes advantage of the act, then we in Nova Scotia must still pay our proportionate share to provide for the poor in that one province that does come in. That certainly seems an unfair proposition, to me at any rate. The deduction from this would appear to me to be that this government should assume the entire responsibility for a pension scheme. The government ought to be willing to go far enough to make it a national undertaking, relieving the provinces and the municipalities of the work which they are at present doing, and substituting therefor a better performance on the part of the national administration of Canada. Someone may ask me why I make that suggestion. Well, the suggestion may be justified on the ground that, according to the information which has been given us, this country is at present in a prosperous condition. If it is in a prosperous condition, and if we have been able to raise twenty-five or thirty million dollars more in the way of taxation than we were able to secure the year before, then on that hypothesis alone the government, it seems to me, ought to assume full responsibility in this matter.
The people of Nova Scotia are to-day fairly well taking care of their poor, particularly in my own constituency; and I rather fancy that the major good of this bill, if it passes and if some of the provinces adopt similar legislation, will be to provide for certain poor people in industrial centres where the indigent at present are not being cared for as well as they ought to be. With the desire to take care of these people I am in perfect accord. But unless the whole country is to bear the responsibility, unless the scheme is to be made Dominion-wide and a national undertaking, I certainly do not feel that we are justified in proceeding with it on the basis of one province or more being obliged to contribute whether or not they benefit. I think I am expressing in this the views held generally by the people of my constituency.
During the last five or six years we have had to shoulder in one part of my constituency $55,000 of extra taxation as a result of maladministration in that county alone, and in Nova Scotia generally we have exhausted practically all our sources of revenue. The
outgoing government left the province in debt to the extent of $1,800,000 odd and the incoming administration, despite all its economies, is still unable to balance its budget. Under these circumstances, and in view of the fact that the municipalities themselves are bearing a heavy burden already, I do not feel like supporting another measure which will require them to contribute thirty-five or forty thousand dollars to such a scheme as this. I may have something later on to say with regard to changes which it may be desirable to make in some of the other clauses of the bill, but in what I have just stated in a general way I believe I am but representing the views held by the people of my constituency.

There is probably one point on which we all agree, and that is that something is necessary in the way of old age pension legislation. Section 5, now under discussion, is of importance. It practically declares that this shall be a non-contributory scheme, and this is the one thing upon which there will no doubt be disagreement between the provinces. For this reason, I think, it would have been wise for the government to have consulted the representatives of the several provinces before draughting and introducing this legislation. It is questionable whether this is the wisest form of legislation for a young and growing country like Canada. Is it advisable, in a young country such as this, to create by means of an act of this kind the impression that individual provision for old age is unnecessary because the government will provide it? The principle, I think, is wrong; and this is the argument which I believe some of the provinces will put forward. In my opinion it would be better to seek a method of inducing people to provide from their earnings for protection of old age. In this regard I believe clause 5 will fall down. Had the provinces been called together in conference some system might have been adopted that would work satisfactorily; and in any case such a conference should have been called. Personalty I am inclined to favour the scheme suggested by the hon. member for West Calgary (Mr. Bennett) the other evening, that of adopting a scheme of old age pensions, and such a scheme instead of being separate might be made a part of the existing annuities system. Under this system a man can very easily set aside during the earning period of his life sufficient funds by small payments which at the age of seventy will provide for him an annuity equal to or much better than the pension proposed in

this legislation. I think our Annuities Act should be studied by every member of the House. I must admit that until the hon. member for West Calgary drew it to my attention I was quite ignorant of aill the benefits to be derived from its operation. I believe that probably seventy-five per cent of our people are not aware of the provisions of that act. If that system of annuities was better known I think it would fee taken advantage of to a far greater extent, and in that way would help to relieve the very situation we are trying to provide for under this measure.
Now, at the present time we know that from all over the Dominion there is a call from many aged people for immediate relief, and I am of opinion that the source of that relief should be the federal government by working out a scheme of old age pensions in connection with out annuity system.
Let me point out wherein I think this proposed legislation falls down. I do not wish it to be understood that I am opposing the principle of old age pensions. I should like to get together with the other members and work out some scheme that would be in the interests of those people who require relief and at the same time keep in mind the interests of the country generally. Each of the provinces is expected to co-operate in carrying out this legislation, and after it is enacted the right hon. Prime Minister has stated that it will be submitted to the provinces in order that they may take it under consideration. This is exactly the scheme worked out in nearly every case where one power is assisting some other power by way of contribution. We in Ontario are familiar with the assistance given in the building of highways. I must say I agree very largely with' what my hon. friend has been saying. Personally I should like to see something added to the bill which would help to ensure the object that he has in view. Section 17 reads as follows:
On or before the thirtieth day of April in each year the Minister of Finance shall make a full report to parliament of the operation of the agreements made pursuant of this act and of the moneys of Canada paid to the provinces under each of the several agreements entered into pursuant hereto.
By presenting that report parliament will have a knowledge of what agreements have been made and what amounts shall be required for subsequent years. I think that wherever an agreement is made, it would be wise that the minister should be required to ask parliament for the grant of money that may be necessary year by year for the purpose; but until some agreement is arrived at I think it would be premature to ask the House to appropriate a sum which cannot possibly be estimated in advance. Take for example this year: were we to seek to make provision by an estimate we would be utterly at a loss. Between now and the next fiscal year it would be quite impossible to say what amount will be required; but once a province has come to us and asked us to make an agreement, and an agreement has been entered into then, I think, thereafter there ought to be some obligation on the government of the day to see that parliament has an opportunity of considering the necessary appropriations and unless there be good and sufficient reason to the contrary of voting them annually. I do not like the House to get away from the annual vote if that can be prevented.

Let me just suggest a
change in the wording and then place my further argument. I would suggest a substitution-I am not moving this, Mr. Chairman, I am merely suggesting it-to this effect:
All sums payable to any province in pursuance of any agreement made under this act shall be paid out of moneys appropriated from time to time by parliament, for that purpose.
That is following almost precisely the wording of a bill we passed this afternoon in regard to another matter. Now, there is no possibility of any demand being made this year. The legislatures of the provinces will not meet until next winter, or next fall, so that no act can be passed by them until just about the same time as this parliament will be again assembled in its next session. No province, therefore, need be worried about this year. But between now and next year the government, we will say, enters into some agreement with a province. Then it can come before parliament next year with an estimate. In the interim should a contingency arise where money is required, the power having already been given, the government can issue a Governor General's warrant for the necessary amount. I would not expect there would be any need whatever to do that between now and next session, but it is the-principle that I am contending for. I know the same principle is quite dear to the heart.

Would that apply to the resolutions read to the House by the member for New Westminster yesterday, from the Soldiers' associations? Would the Governor in Council have power under this paragraph to make the regulations include the class of persons referred to by the hon. member?
No.

Is it not desirable
that they should be included?

I said a moment
ago that I did not think it desirable to bring it in under this bill as a special clause. If it is necessary to give returned men special consideration, let it be done by special legislation, but do not bring them as a class under this bill. I think that would be a mistake.

Will the minister explain clause (c):
The Governor in Council shall have power. . . to provide by regulation, for. . . the definition of residence and of the intervals of absence from Canada or a province by which residence therein shall not be deemed to have been interrupted.
We have already gone through several clauses dealing with the question of residence.
I would take it that clause 19 gives an added power which may vary the provisions of the other clauses that have been already passed.
Is that correct ?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
In regard to
all these sections, my hon. friends will realize that it is impossible to anticipate the hundred and one different. matters that will come up, and all that has been attempted, by outlining the different matters specially mentioned, is to make it clear that it is desirable to note in advance as many as possible, but at the same time to leave room for additional phases of the question which may have to be the subject of regulation. In reference to a question asked as to residence, I can answer it by giving an illustration. Take the case of trade commissioners, who might have occasion to spend four years in Africa, Australia, or some country other than Canada. They would be absent from Canada for four years, and nobody is going to think of their case until the time arrives when the question of pension has to be settled. That would be one of the cases which would come under this provision. The Governor in Council would have power to provide by regulation for the definition of residence, and of the intervals of absence from Canada or from a province by which residence therein shall not be deemed to have been interrupted. The applicant is supposed to be five years in the province and twenty years in Canada. During that period he might be four years abroad on the business of the country, and under this clause regulations could be made to meet that case. I understand that all these paragraphs set out here are taken in large part from the British legislation, and they are included in order to anticipate matters of that kind which it is impossible to cover in a general clause.

Clause 19 says that the
Governor in Council shall have power to make regulations not inconsistent with the provisions of the act.
Paragraph (c) agreed to.
Paragraph (d) agreed to.
Old Age Pensions

On section 19, paragraph (e)-Determination of income.

In view of the very
complicated clauses we dealt with previously as to turning over the pensioner's house to the pension authorities, the renting of the house, its sale after the pensioner dies, and so forth, I think it would be much better to give the pension authority power to assess the annual value of any residence owned by the petitioner instead of having all these complicated provisions about taking it over. Surely we do not want to become the custodian of a lot of dwelling houses and pay the taxes on them. I would just take arbitrary authority to assess what the property is worth by way of rental. It would be infinitely simpler than this.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; Minister of Labour
speechtext:
That is exactly what is
done in Ontario by the municipality in the case of any property owned by an occupant of the House of Refuge.

That is very simple.
There is a 'legal provision in regard to it. We do not want to keep track of property all over the Dominion, keep the houses in repair and pay taxes. We do not want to assume that burden.
Paragraph (e) agreed to.
Paragraph (f) agreed to.
On section 19, paragraph (g)-Under treatment in public institutions.

During the previous discussion some hon. member, speaking with authority stated that it was the intention of the government under the provisions of this act to make an agreement with the province that would enable the federal authorities to pay this pension to the province on behalf, we will say, of institutions like poorhouses or old men's homes, such as we have in British Columbia. Is it the intention of the government to do that? Will the government disclose what it had in its mind when this clause was draughted?

This would probably cover cases where the pensioner required to go to the hospital for treatment, or to some public institution of that kind, in which case a portion of his pension would be payable to the institution. I think that is a matter that would have to be worked out pretty well by the pension authorities. The province might be able to maintain some of these pensioners at less cost and to greater advantage to the pensioner in an institution like 
an old men's home, in which case the pension could be partly used for his maintenance.
This is the most important clause of the bill.
Oh, no.

This is the clause that
will really be operative if the bill ever becomes law. The provinces have these institutions; some of them are very fine ones, and the provinces are not going to scrap them and then assume the burden of helping to maintain these people.
Is it the intention of subsection (g) to provide for the payment of the pension or any part of it to the institution in which the beneficiary is placed?
Yes.

It does not say so in the
clause. It says, "the circumstances in which pensions may be paid for the benefit of persons supported or under treatment in public institutions." If- you are paying the money to the person himself, you are paying it for his benefit. The clause says, "supported or under treatment in public institutions." There is nothing in the clause to provide that the pension be paid to the institution.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; Minister of Labour
speechtext: That is broad enough to cover everything, I should say.

Too broad. Surely the wording of the clause is consistent with payment to the person, and does not neces-
11 p.m. sarily imply payment to the institution. You should expressly say in the clause that there is power to pay it to the institution.

We pay over our money to the province. It may be that under certain circumstances the province will find it to the advantage of the pensioner, to the advantage of the province and of the whole scheme, to pay part of the pension to the public institution in which the pensioner is placed. It depends on the circumstances.
If the intention of the clause is to empower the federal government to pay either to the individual or to someone else, the language does not seem to convey that intention.
We pay only to the province.
That is a different matter.

Is there anything in this paragraph in conflict with section 16, which provides that no pension shall be sub-

Old Age Pensions
ject to alienation or transfer by the pensioner or to seizure in satisfaction of any claim against him?
No.
My hon. friend may as well be clear on that point. As I read paragraph (g) the meaning is that the money will not go to the individual at all, but to the institution in which he happens to be living.
That is the very question I asked, and I was told that the money did not go to the institution at all, but that it rested with the province to say to whom it should go-

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; Minister of Labour
speechtext: The federal government pays only to the province.

The minister is not answering the question dearly; my hon. friend (Mr. Bury) gets one understanding and I another. The straight question is this: Is it the intention to provide in these regulations that the federal portion of the pension may be paid to the province on behalf of an institution just as well as on behalf of the individual?

As I understand it, our share goes to the province, but the regulations will provide the circumstances under which the money shall be paid by the province to the institution rather than to the pensioner. I repeat, it is the most important clause in the whole act; it is the one which will really work if the act goes into operation. We shall! be helping to keep the poor in the homes.

If it is intended to incorporate in the bill power on the part of the federal government to direct where the money shall go, whether to the beneficiary or to the institution, this intention is not being expressed clearly enough in the phrase "the circumstances in which pensions may be paid."

The pension may be paid by the province for the benefit of the individual.
(Mr. BURY: When you pay the money to the province you are not paying it for the benefit of the individual if the province hands it over to the institution.

The Dominion
government pays the money directly to the province, and the province may decide under certain circumstances that it is to the advantage of the pensioner that the payment should be made to the institution for his keep.
Then what is the use of paragraph (g) at all if you pay the money to the province and allow the province to do as it likes with it?

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; Minister of Labour
speechtext:
The scheme must be approved by the federal government before the agreement is entered into.
Paragraph (g) agreed to.
On section 19, paragraph (h)-The mode in which pensions are to be payable.

What does this
mean?
Kootenay): This is a matter of regulation.
Does it mean that the pension may be payable by promissory note, by cheque or in cash?
We hope that the Post Office Department may be utilized in the payment of the moneys. The necessary arrangements will have to be worked out.
I take it, then, that it refers to the department of government through which the pensions will be paid?
It merely provides for the machinery through which payment will be made.

So far as the Yukon and the Northwest go I have no hope at all that this act will apply to them, notwithstanding the assurance of the Minister of Public Works that it is the intention of the government that it shall. Certainly, as the bill is worded, there is no evidence that such is the intention.

It was intimated this afternoon that there would be an amendment to clear up any doubt my hon. friend might have in this regard. Before we go out of committee to-night we shall move an amendment for the purpose.
Paragraph (h) agreed to.
Section 19, paragraphs (i) to (m) inclusive, agreed to.
On section 19, paragraph (n)-Recovery of pension payments made by reason of nondisclosure of facts or innocent or false representations.

Is this not an encroachment upon provincial property rights? If you try to recover from a man in Alberta or Saskatchewan a pension wrongfully paid to him by reason of misrepresentation or concealment of facts,.
Old Age Pensions

are you not thereby trenching on provincial rights? It seems to me that you are dealing with a question that lies purely within the purview of the provincial legislature, and you are doing so by order in council.
The provinces will have to agree.

But there is the whole trouble with the very conception of this bill. The Governor in Council cannot make regulations to govern the recovery of pension payments, with or without interest, for the simple reason that, as pointed out by the hon. member (Mr. Bury), the government of Canada cannot recover. But the Governor in Council can take the stand that it must first be satisfied with the provincial statute. The suggestion I made first of all, therefore, should have have been accepted, that the provincial statute must be approved by the Governor in Council. Then the provincial statute will not be approved until it so provides. But you can never by regulation of the Governor in Council provide for something which only a provincial government can do. In a word, this is a conglomeration borrowed from a statute which cannot apply because we have a federal system, and they have not.
The provinces can always delegate their powers to the federal government.
They are never going to do it.
They might do so.
Does the Solicitor General imagine the provinces are going to authorize the federal government to come in and recover pensions that the provinces have paid?
I do not say they would, but from the legal viewpoint they could.

I suppose from the legal viewpoint they could authorize Mars to do it; but it is inconceivable. What is the sense of suggesting that the Governor in Council may make regulations for the recovery of money when only the province can recover it? The province can provide by its bill or by regulations under its bill, and those regulations should be approved by the Governor in Council here. That is a suggestion I made in reference to clause 5, but the ministry brushed it aside. If they had done that they could take a knife and slash out about two-thirds of the clauses under 19. As it is, there they are, just surplusage.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; Minister of Labour
speechtext: Does it not strike my right hon. friend that the provisions are to be made by the Governor in Council as to the circum-stnces under which these payments should be recovered? For instance, he says to the other party to this agreement: You shall recover from a certain pensioner payments made to him by reason of false representations. In other words, this government does not propose to allow the pensioner who obtains a pension under false representations to retain it, and under certain circumstances it shall be recovered. It is all part of the agreement.
Very well, if it is part of the agreement how can it be a subject of regulation?

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; Minister of Labour
speechtext:
The Governor in Council
says by one of his regulations:	This is the
agreement you make, you must recover pensions that were obtained under false representations.

The agreement is something signed between the two governments, and once it is signed no regulation has anything to do with it. I can see how that came to be put in there, and the minister ought to acknowledge it. It is in the British act. That act says that the King in Council can make regulations for the recovery of pensions which they paid. That is why it is there. But there is no place for it here because we cannot recover the pension. It is true we can say the provincial legislature must pass such and such a law. That is all provided for by section 5, or should be, by the simple assertion that a provincial statute and the regulations thereunder shall be satisfactory to the governor in council.
Paragraphs (n) to (r) agreed to.
Section 19 agreed to.

There is no use making
a suggestion. These most anomalous clauses indicate that the government never expect them to go into effect.
On section 20-When regulations come into effect.

It is harmless.
Section 20 agreed to.
Now the amendments.

May I suggest that whatever amendments the government have to offer might first be proposed, then we can adjourn and consider them.

Opium and Narcotic Drug Act

The first amendment, I think, will not require very much discussion. It deals with the Yukon Territory. It is proposed to amend section 2 (d) by adding the words:
-in respect to which "commissioner" shall be read for "lieutenant governor in council".

The amendment is to
bring that about?

Yes, I think it
covers that without any difficulty.

Mr. Chairman, the
minister will have to go a great deal further than that to make this 'bill applicable to the Yukon Territory and the Northwest Territories; in fact, even ,to make it workable anywhere in Canada. Stemmed up, this bill simply means that the Dominion government pay back to the provinces fifty per cent of the amount they pay out on old age pensions to the persons enumerated. The Yukon Territory and the Northwest Territories with their scattered population are not going to enact any legislation under which they will pay out old age pensions and come back to the federal government under this bill for fifty per cent of those payments.

Then they are
not in the scheme.

No. In the last
campaign the government candidate in Yukon Territory, a personal friend of the Minister of Public Works, made a great point of saying to the electors:	The government has
in view an old age pension bill. Not an old age pension bill that would not apply to the Yukon, but a bill that would; and evidently the government did have that in mind. Formerly one of the main reasons why this old age pensions legislation could not get ahead was because the government of Canada could not get co-operation from the provinces. As regards the Yukon and the 'Northwest Territories they do not need any co-operation, because the federal government governs those territories regardless of any provincial governments, they are typically federal territories, and if this government is sincere in wishing to put into effect old age pensions there, why not go ahead and do it? Do not hamper any such scheme with the provisions wrapped around the provinces. The Yukon Territory and the Northwest Territories are federal territories, not hampered by provincial governments. You either want to give them old age pensions or you do not. I say to the minister, if he wishes he can make this bill applicable
to the Yukon Territory and the Northwest Territories and give them old age pensions. This bill will never apply there; it will be inoperative. It will not even catch any votes-it does not go that far.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health; Minister of Labour
speechtext: Nobody is concerned about votes under this bill.

Mr. Chairman, I think
we have had a pretty prosperous evening; we have gone through this bill very carefully and have allowed several clauses to stand. I would suggest to the minister in charge of the bill and to the Prime Minister that the amendments which might clear up the misunderstandings in the first four or five clauses should be prepared carefully and presented at another sitting, when they can be dealt with.

Mr. Chairman. I
move that the committee rise and report progress.
Progress reported.
